idiom_name: state-owning handler struct + named html/template fragments executed with explicit data
implementation_notes: Go has no component tree; the container is a struct (or a small package) that owns the state and exposes methods, while the stateless children are named templates executed with an explicit data argument - `{{template "cart-lines" .Lines}}` inside a page template, or `ExecuteTemplate(w, "cart-lines", lines)` from a handler. Nothing inside a template can reach global state, so a child is renderable from a literal struct in a golden-file test. Use html/template (contextual escaping) rather than text/template when the output is HTML, and keep request-scoped state out of package-level variables.
pitfalls: Parsing templates after the first Execute fails, and executing shared templates while another goroutine still defines them races: parse everything once at startup, then treat the set as read-only.
Package-level state, or text/template with template.HTML, defeats the split: the child renders whatever the global holds and unescaped values become an XSS hole.
Passing the whole handler or the *http.Request into a child template invites markup to call methods with side effects; pass a small view struct with exactly the fields the child needs.
